newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Schindler business starts well in 1997.
newsitem.headline: Schindler business starts well in 1997.

text.p: Schindler Holding AG said 1997 had started well and it was confident of achieving its stated goal of 1997 net profit of 160 million Swiss francs, before restructuring costs of 25 million.
"The year 1997 has started well and new orders are going as planned," Peter Szbinden, president of the main elevators and escalators business, told Schindler's annual news conference.
"The quality of prices is stable, although still at a relatively low level," Szbinden added.

Schindler, the world's largest maker of escalators and the second-largest elevator maker, saw world prices for its products slump in the mid-1990s due to recessions in major markets and a gruelling price war with its world rivals.
Earlier Schindler said it expected a net profit of 160 million Swiss francs this year before estimated restructuring charges of 25 million.
"We have no doubt at the moment that we will achieve this goal for 1997," chief financial officer Alfred Spoerri also said.
Spoerri said the company would be reporting a first half net profit for the first time this year in an interim report due in August.
But he cautioned the net profit figure would be less than half of the year's targeted goal because the first half of each year was traditionally weaker in performance than the second half.

Spoerri said the operating margin in 1996, before extraordinary costs for restructuring, was 3.4 percent, up from 2.8 percent in 1995, but still only about one-third of the comparative margin at chief rival Otis Elevator Co, a unit of United Technologies Corp.
"We still have to catch up quite a bit to the best of the class (Otis)," Spoerri told the news conference.

Szbinden said the outlook for this year was based partly on a line of new products being launched. These included a low price model 001 in Italy, a new 9300 escalator line and a world premiere breakthrough in elevator technology due to be presented in Munich, Germany on April 15.
"I expect very good market acceptance for these products," Szbinden said.
